Q: Is a macro-based integer “type-builder” API (e.g. INT(32), UINT(16), OPTIMAL) a practical, portable replacement for stdint.h? A:

Many projects did (and still do) build their own integer layers on top of the language, and in that sense this idea is not entirely new. The motivation here is not to re-invent pre-stdint typedefs, but to understand whether there are recurring pain points that still cause developers to wrap or rename stdint.h today, and whether a more expressive, intent-oriented abstraction could reduce that duplication in a standardized way. If the consensus is that simple aliases like typedef uint32_t UINT32; already solve the problem well enough, that’s also valuable feedback for evaluating whether a more structured approach would actually add real-world value or just historical déjà vu.

Q: How many processes are created with these fork() statements? A:

Process

Fork #1

  • Original parent calls fork(), creating 1 child.
  • Both parent and child continue independently.

Fork #2

  • Both existing processes call fork().
  • Each creates 1 child.
  • Total processes: 4

Fork #3

  • All 4 processes call fork().
  • Each creates 1 child.
  • Total processes: 8

Conditional Fork #4 (if (pid == 0))

  • Only the children created by fork #3 execute this fork.
  • Each creates 1 child.
  • Total processes after this step: 12

Fork #5 (Unconditional)

  • Every existing process calls fork().
  • Each creates 1 child, doubling the process count.
  • Final total processes: 24

Q: How to read/write in minio using spark? A:

That error usually means Spark’s S3A client ended up with a blank/invalid endpoint host (so when it builds the HTTP client it tries to create an HttpHost with hostname = null). With MinIO + Hadoop 3.3.x, the most reliable fix is to set (1) the credentials provider, (2) the region, and (3) ensure the endpoint is applied to Hadoop conf.

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = (
    SparkSession.builder
    .appName("spark-minio")
    # --- S3A / MinIO ---
    .config("spark.hadoop.fs.s3a.endpoint", "http://obj_storage:9000")
    .config("spark.hadoop.fs.s3a.path.style.access", "true")
    .config("spark.hadoop.fs.s3a.connection.ssl.enabled", "false")

    # IMPORTANT: force simple static creds provider
    .config("spark.hadoop.fs.s3a.aws.credentials.provider",
            "org.apache.hadoop.fs.s3a.SimpleAWSCredentialsProvider")
    .config("spark.hadoop.fs.s3a.access.key", "minioadmin")
    .config("spark.hadoop.fs.s3a.secret.key", "minioadmin")

    # IMPORTANT: set a region (MinIO commonly uses us-east-1)
    .config("spark.hadoop.fs.s3a.endpoint.region", "us-east-1")

    # optional but fine
    .config("spark.hadoop.fs.s3a.impl", "org.apache.hadoop.fs.s3a.S3AFileSystem")
    .getOrCreate()
)

df = spark.read.csv("s3a://client-files/movie_review.csv", header=True, inferSchema=True)
df.show()

Why these extra configs matter

  • fs.s3a.aws.credentials.provider: without this, S3A may try other credential chains (env/instance/profile). In containers this can behave oddly and you can end up with a partially-initialized client.

  • fs.s3a.endpoint.region: newer AWS SDK behavior + S3A can require a region to build/sign requests cleanly (MinIO is happy with us-east-1).

Quick sanity checks (inside the spark container)

  1. Confirm DNS/network:
  • curl http://obj_storage:9000/minio/health/ready
  1. Confirm the object path is exactly:

  • bucket: client-files

  • object key: movie_review.csv (at bucket root)

If you run executors (not just local driver)

If you later run Spark in a real cluster mode, make sure these same spark.hadoop.fs.s3a.* configs are visible to both driver and executors (e.g., pass them via spark-submit --conf ... or spark-defaults.conf), otherwise the driver may be configured but executors won’t be.

If you apply the provider + region + endpoint exactly as above, the “hostname cannot be null” issue typically disappears and reads/writes to MinIO start working.
